Love anything related to the theory of computation and always looking to discuss Turing if anyone wants to slide into my DMs 🙂 Hello everyone! my name is raffiq, self taught programmer in Malaysia. I was a mechanical engineera and have been into blockhain since 2019. decided to change my path into programmer and dedicate my time fully into this space. I have made a few Dapps and took a learning certs course in blockchain developer from Udacity. Passionate in learning this tech. I was told about this program and very much interested in joining this and dedicate my time to this! I have a question, how important is it for one need to fully understand the yellow paper in order to be in this program? Hey I'm trying to understand the snapshot system in geth with no luck. I'm wondering if other clients have a similar system. I believe openethereum uses the snapshot system for their "warp" sync Sadly I haven't learned rust I've only played with geth. Do other clients all have their own storage and db system? This is interesting: https://t.co/Yhvjpq0DO8 awesome, will have a look now. Thanks what made you change your mind on ETH? I used to work in architecture and design as well! welcome A variety of things. I went fairly in depth in my application. I was originally a Bitcoin maxi. I thought its simplicity was what helped it to work so well. I thought having a Turing-complete language like Eth does introduced more flaws than benefits. I didn't see too many use cases for smart contracts either. Eth seemed like Bitcoin but with lots of extra bells and whistles but lacking in novelty. I also worked in cybersecurity briefly in university and read about security vulnerabilities in smart contracts and such.. That began to change once we got into last Summer and saw many DeFi projects built on Ethereum which began offering services typically done by traditional financial intermediaries as well as reading about Eth 2.0 which seeks to streamline many aspects of the protocol which began to convince me that the developers of Eth really were serious about building something that worked, was secure, and revolutionary. I hope that answers your question. Need advice. I have been out of touch with math for some time, though I studied engineering in college. What specific topics would you recommend to brush up to understand the math in the yellow paper? Thanks. Maybe some discrete math. The fourth section goes through the notation Wood uses throughout. Yet he provides a few simple equations prior to this. The yellow paper cheat sheet I think would probably help you a lot if you can sort of look at them both side by side. By fourth section you mean "Blocks, State and Transactions"? And by cheat sheet did you mean this one: https://github.com/benjaminion/YellowPaper_CheatSheet/blob/master/YPCheatSheet.pdf ? sorry if i pardon if i asked silly ques FWIW, I don't think you need to refresh any specific area. excerpts.author: sabnock
excerpts.content: A variety of things. I went fairly in depth in my application. I was originally a Bitcoin maxi. I thought its simplicity was what helped it to work so well. I thought having a Turing-complete language like Eth does introduced more flaws than benefits. I didn't see too many use cases for smart contracts either. Eth seemed like Bitcoin but with lots of extra bells and whistles but lacking in novelty. I also worked in cybersecurity briefly in university and read about security vulnerabilities in smart contracts and such.. That began to change once we got into last Summer and saw many DeFi projects built on Ethereum which began offering services typically done by traditional financial intermediaries as well as reading about Eth 2.0 which seeks to streamline many aspects of the protocol which began to convince me that the developers of Eth really were serious about building something that worked, was secure, and revolutionary.
